Before this matter is further pro-



Bank of Canada
ceeded with I think I should say to the hon. gentleman who proposes the bill that perhaps he is not aware of the fact that under the international agreement made between various countries, including Canada, regarding silver, there is an obligation undertaken by Canada that the government shall purchase or otherwise arrange for withdrawing from the market, as in the attached memorandum of agreement, 1,671,802 fine ounces of silver in each calendar year beginning with the calendar year 1934. The agreement does not terminate until the first of January, 1938, and I hardly think that the hon. gentleman would desire, by the legislation which he now contemplates, to endeavour to destroy the international agreement to which I have referred.

If I may refer to the point raised by the Prime Minister, I submit with all respect that the legislation proposed to be introduced by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) does not in the slightest degree interfere with the agreement to which the right hon. gentleman has referred. It only implements it and strengthens it, proposing that the Bank of Canada shall not have less than that actual amount specified in that agreement. With respect to the point raised by my right hon. friend yesterday, I submit that this cannot possibly affect either revenue or expenditure as suggested, nor can it affect the Bank of Canada even if, Mr. Speaker, you construe the Bank of Canada to be the agent of the minister. I think the point raised by the Prime Minister now is raised more or less on grounds of public policy, and I suggest with the utmost deference, after a careful examination of both sections of the proposed bill, that it does not in the slightest degree interfere with the international agreement; an the contrary, it seeks definitely to implement the terms of that agreement.

I am going to ask the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) if he will allow this matter to stand for another day. I may say that I have given the matter very careful consideration and I am in considerable doubt as to whether or not the bill is in order, but I certainly do not wish to rule that it is out of order unless I satisfy my own mind on the subject. On section 1-Power to prescribe fees for inspection.

Might I ask the minister
why he is making this amendment to section 17 which deals with fish and shellfish canneries and1 their inspection? It seems to me that it should have been made to section 18 which deals with fish and shellfish packed in cans. The minister is aware that inspection of canneries lies no longer with the dominion but with the provincial authorities and this section is reaLly obsolete. The amendment would seem to be more appropriate if it were made as an addition to section 18 of the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The object of the amending bill is to clear up any doubt which may have existed as to whether under this section the government have power to collect fees. The insertion of the clause as suggested, appears to me to meet the difficulty. It states:
The governor in council may from time to time prescribe a tariff of fees that shall be charged for the inspection of canned fish and shellfish.
And attached to section 17, it appears to me to be quite appropriate.

Surely the minister did not catch my meaning. I am not finding fault with the wording of the clause in the bill. I am merely saying that it is being put into the wrong place. It is being attached' to a section which has no standing in law to-day. Section. 17 reads:
All fish and shellfish canneries shall be inspected as provided by the regulations.
But that is ultra -vires of the jurisdiction of the dominion at the present time and has been since the decision of the privy council somewhere around 1927 or 1928. It would seem appropriate to put it in the proper place instead of the wrong place. I admit it would have sufficient significance wherever it is put, but it would be much more appropriate to put it in the section that is within our jurisdiction, section 18, dealing with canned fish, rather than in the one dealing with canneries over which we have no jurisdiction.

Hon. ROBERT WEIR (Minister of Agriculture) moved the second reading of Bill No. 72, to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act.
Motion agreed to, bill the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Morand in the chair.
On section 1-Definitions.
Would the minister give a word of explanation as to what the changes are?

The changes are, first, to leave no doubt as to meat, not only for export but also for interprovincial trade, being included for inspection. Also in order that packers' yards through which direct shipments are made to packing plants may, if necessary, be brought under the same regulations as public stockyards; to give effect to the recommendations of the price spreads commission.
Is not export from one province to another taken care of by the present inspection in meat packing plants? Is it the intention to bring the small butcher doing a domestic business under it?
No.
Well, what is the idea concerning trade between province and province?

At present the act defines "live stock products" as including meat for export, but that does not cover interprovincial trade. The definition "for export" has been changed to include inter-provicial trade.

That is what I am asking. What will be the position of a farmer who lives on the boundary line between two provinces, or a local butcher who slaughters say in Alberta and sells the meat in Saskatchewan? It is not now inspected because it does not go through a packing house. Will he be an offender under the act if he does that?
No.

Well, in that case there is not much use making the change,
if it can be evaded as easily as that.

Live Stock Act

There are many plants that are not inspected establishments. At the present time there is only provision for inspection of plants doing interprovincial trade, but not of the product itself in transit. It will not in any way affect these small butcher shops.

I think the minister will admit that there is not very much to this bill. I do not suppose it is meant to be one of the reforms bills at all, just the regular dressing up that usually takes place from time to time in these measures as circumstances require. Section 1 that we are now discussing defines "export," and the meaning is the same as it has been all along. "Export" has meant export out of the country and also interprovincial trade.
Then the other changes have grown out of that to some extent; such as the definition of what "domestic consumption" means. These are very trifling amendments but they are necessary. I do not despise them, but they do not by any means conform to the majority report of the price spreads commission. When the Minister of Justice was dealing with the amendments to the criminal code the other day he seemed to be very anxious as nearly as possible to follow along the lines of the price spreads report, which seems to be looked upon as the sacred ark of the covenant; but in this bill the minister seems to be getting away from the recommendations of the price spreads commission as far as possible. Maybe he is right in that respect. One recommendation of the majority report as I recollect is that there should be a live stock marketing board appointed. I do not see anything of that in this bill; perhaps the minister will explain why it is not here. I am not criticizing him for it not being here, I do not think it will be missed; at the same time I would like to understand why the Minister of Justice is so religiously desirous of carrying out in every detail the price spreads report, even to the point of absurdity, in the amendments to the criminal code.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Oh no.
Well, pretty nearly. My good friend the Minister of Agriculture seems to disregard it by overlooking the major report of the price spreads committee on the live stock industry.

Provision is being made, with the exception of those amendments, to give effect to the recommendations of the price spreads report. The hon. member who has just taken his seat was right in his suggestion in that connection.
Are we through with section 1?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not yet.
Then I shall wait until we are before saying anything further.
May I ask the minister if a man taking meat across an interprovincial boundary must fill in reports and give information or call at any office to get permission to do such a thing?
No. But if complaints are made and abuses arise this gives power for action to be taken.
Has the minister anything definite in mind, any particular regulation that he proposes to make under this section?
With respect to hogs passing from one province to another it might be necessary to take certain action.

In what way? It would be interesting to know whether there is anything definite in the mind of the minister or of the department as to what is to be done under this section. From reading it I do not know just what is aimed at.

One example might be the failure to observe grading regulations in connection with hogs, for example, or anything else that might arise in this connection. The whole point in the change of this definition is to give further power not only in connection with exports but also in connection with interprovincial trade in order to correct any abuses that may arise.

That does not say anything at all. We do not know what abuse the legislation is designed to remove or what offence is expected to be created under it or what punishment there is to be for the offence; in fact we are entirely in the dark as to what the government have in mind. Does the department intend to prevent certain kinds of meat from moving from province to province while they may be moved from point to point within a province? Is that the point they have in mind?
Previous to this amendment "export" meant only international trade. The definition is changed here to include interprovincial trade, to which the same regulations can apply.
What kind of regulations; regulation in what way?

In any connection, either as to inspection or any of the powers
Live Stock Act

contained in this act, that previously applied only to export for international trade. Now they will apply to interprovincial trade.
What provisions do apply to export trade?
That is given in the regulations, which I have not here.

I should like to support
the objection to this section of my hon. friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). I think there is danger in creating barriers between the provinces. I believe what we should have in mind in Canada is the development of a national sentiment instead of the creation of different provincial territories separated and divided one from the other. If you start with small matters such as this in connection with the regulation of cattle, hogs and so on it may spread to other fields, and I think that is a dangerous principle to develop in this country.

In the explanatory note a
reference is made to the recommendation in clause 11 of division 2 on page XXII of the report. So far as I can see that is an incorrect reference; I cannot find the recommendation referred to. I should like to know what recommendation is referred to so that I may see what the government have in mind.
This reference deals specifically with the grading of meats.

Where is the reference? It
is incorrectly stated in the explanatory notes.

I am referring to
the reference now, "consumer grades for meats."
What page is that?

Page XXII of the preface. Recommendations have come to the department from time to time, and the department itself has also felt, that in connection with meats it would be advisable to make available to the provinces, if they so desired, an inspection of meats for domestic purposes. A good deal of work has been done in connection with the grading of meats during the past number of years with the hope that if the consumers had some assurance as to the quality of the meat they were purchasing, through a grade placed upon it-red label or blue label beef, for example-it would encourage the consumption of meat. I think perhaps it has come to the attention of every hon. member of the house, in travelling throughout the country and stopping at hotels and other eating places, that possibly nine

times out of ten they have been disappointed in the quality of the meat served to them, particularly beef. I know that opinion is held very strongly by the live stock producers themselves, and each person who is disappointed in the quality of the meat he gets is a lost purchaser, to a certain extent, of live stock products. So far this inspection has not been pressed in the domestic market but it is felt that if the province of Ontario, for example, should wish to carry further this policy of grading meats for consumption, they should be given the privilege of doing so.
Personally I feel that because of the large percentage of our meat, for instance beef, that is consumed locally, it would not take very much of a stepping up in the consumption to take care of a great part of our present surplus for export, and it is felt that the one move that would go further than anything else to bring about that end would be to make it easier for the consumer to be assured of the grade or quality of his meat, so that the purchaser might know as nearly as possible what he was getting. I believe during the investigation by the price spreads committee complaints were registered that stores would advertise for sale red label and blue label beef. These stores would have some of that beef for sale but on some occasions, without an explanation to the purchaser, they sold beef that was not graded either red or blue label. In that way the consumer was misled, with no possibility of redress. I know there is a very strong feeling among those who are anxious to make better use of our domestic market that we should carry further the grading of beef in order to encourage thp consumption of higher quality beef and to make more difficult the misrepresentation that undoubtedly has occurred in some cases in this regard. In order to do that the definition of "export" has to be changed in order to take care of the interprovincial movement; so that if the province of Ontario decided to have compulsory provincial inspection of beef, for example, that would not be effective if beef could be shipped in from other provinces without undergoing the same inspection.

Would the
minister indicate to the committee what percentage of our annual production of various live stock products, including hogs, cattle, sheep, lambs and so on, goes to the export market?
I regret very much that I have not those exact figures with me.

I think they are rather important in view of the minister's

Live Stock Act
observation that a slight stepping, up of the domestic consumption would largely take care of our surplus for export.

That is the point I was endeavouring to make. We have a market for all the lambs we produce, and an export market is unnecessary. Our consumption of beef is in the neighbourhood of 85 per cent of production.
I believe the figures are shown at the bottom of page 145 of the price spreads report.
What percentage is rejected on account of disease?
About one-half of one per cent is rejected and condemned.
Does that apply to beef.
That applies to live stock, as a whole. Dairy cattle run higher than that figure.
A few years ago the percentage of tuberculosis in pork was very high. Has it been decreased?

Some tubercular infection shows in about 20 to 25 per cent of the hogs marketed. In a great number of those cases certain glands in the neck are mildly affected. Those hogs or parts thereof are discarded and not allowed to go into consumption. In my former statement however I did not take that into consideration.
Does the amendment give authority to apply grading regulations to meat in all packing plants engaging in interprovincial business?
Yes.

It makes no difference whether or not all the meat going through a particular packing plant leaves a certain province; it applies to the whole product. The grading applies to the whole product of that packing plant?
That is the intention, yes.

What about meat imported from other dominions into Canada. I am thinking particularly about mutton. It is imported, and I believe is sometimes sold over the counter as Iamb. Having tasted some of the lamb that is sold I have a suspicion that I am correct in my assumption.

If a province decides that all meat within that province shall
be inspected and graded and that no meat within the province may be sold otherwise, this measure gives power to prevent an interprovincial movement of uninspected meat, and would take care of the difficulty mentioned by the hon. member.
Does the act as it stands give the federal government the right to insist upon the grading of mutton or lamb brought into this country from other countries?
I do not think we have power at the present time except as I have explained.

I consider that a very important matter, and on previous occasions have made reference to it in this chamber. H it were possible to have an amendment to the act or to obtain the cooperation- of the provinces in the matter I believe the live stock industry would be greatly helped.

I agree
with the views expressed by the hon. member for Peace River, namely, that if live stock products are to be imported into Canada and are to come in direct competition with our own production it is highly important that they be under a strict system of inspection and grading, the same as domestic products.
In- respect to the question asked a few minutes ago I would refer the committee to the information at the bottom of page 145 of the report. I shall read some of the figures:

These figures indicate clearly that only a very small surplus of domestic production goes into export trade.

I can readily realize that there will not be many cattle raised in Canada for export purposes if the prices remain at the point they have been in the last year or two. Cattle have been sold by the farmers at one-half cent or one cent per pound on the hoof. That price does not pay for their keep, and the farmers are not going to raise many of them. There is not much encouragement for the farmer to go
Live Stock Act

into the production of live stock, and there will not be much difficulty in persuading the Canadian people to eat the total production. I do not think there will be much necessity for grading for export unless the price can be raised.
What will happen in the southern part of the province from which I come when we wish to pass through a customs port to cross the line-because I presume before this session is over we will have a measure of reciprocity with the United States? We have been looking for it for two or three years. This government has promised it and of course it always keeps its promises. When we have that measure of reciprocity cattle will cross the line without duty, and we do not want to have to take them to Moose Jaw, a distance of about 150 miles, to have them graded. We want to have some system of getting through customs ports and across the line without having to make that long trip for grading purposes. Even to-day we are taking cattle across the line in the southern part of the province and are paying the duty. They are being sold in the Chicago market because it pays us to do that. It is better to sell them there than to sell them in Canada. What provision has been made for the grading of cattle going out in that way?

We have power to grade beef cattle leaving the country in that manner, but it has never been exercised. We are doing it in so far as dairy cattle are concerned in connection with shipments going to the United Kingdom. No person regrets more than I do the condition the hon. member has described, namely, the difficulty of getting an export market, and the fact that the market in the United States was lost before the present government took office.

This is a huge joke that the Tories put over on every occasion, namely, the loss of this market. For two evenings we have been treated to a dialogue about the loss of markets. The hon. member who acted as chairman of the price spreads commission was desperately anxious to indicate that the people of Canada could eat the domestic supply. That is the sort of stuff the Tories will feed to the electors at the next election, in the hope that the Canadian people will fail to remember that there was a day when prices were sufficient to warrant production, when we had large amounts of dairy products to export-in one year 24,000,000 pounds. Those >vere days when people drank more milk and ate more butter than they ever did before in the history of Canada.
You remember the Hawley-Smoot tariff?

Yes, I do; and I remember what you said about it. Go back now and tell the same story to your electors, and see whether or not you will be elected. The electors are becoming fed up on this sort of thing. We sit here day after day and listen to hon. members opposite tell us how the market disappeared when the Liberals were in office. What justification has the government for what has happened in the last five years with regard to price reductions, when because of lack of markets production has fallen off? Hon. members opposite have been advising the fellow who wants to eat to tighten up his belt and to eat less. They have advised him to eat less eggs and butter in order that they might take up the slack in home consumption. You have closed every possible market by various devices since you came into office, and I would advise you to go very slow in talking about any restriction of markets because I have in my desk statistics demonstrating how badly the markets both domestic and export have fallen off. So far as the export market is concerned, if prices continue as they are we shall not need any export market or domestic market either because, if present conditions continue, one of these days you will find yourself in the happy position of not having a market and of having no people to eat your products anyway. It will be a Godsend when there is an election and we can have this moribund outfit cleared out and give somebody who will do business for Canada a chance to do it.

Does the hon. member state that during the time his party was in power, when the United States tariff was raised against our cattle to three cents a pound, that did not shut practically the whole of our cattle out from the United States?

May I draw the minister's attention to this fact, that simultaneously with the loss of the American cattle market we secured the British market, and that is where our cattle went to. This government think that they took the embargo off cattle. It is true that they attended to the frills and tagends in the way of restrictions that still remained after 1023, but the major part of the embargo was taken off in 1923 under the Liberal administration. But we never claimed that all the credit belonged to us but to all who had preceded us and had been endeavouring to remove it for thirty

Live Stock Act
years back. Immediately we were shut out from the United States market our market in Great Britain was opened up, and in the second or third year after the embargo was removed, in 19(26, we shipped over 100,000 cattle to Great Britain, which is twice as much as we ever shipped since. So when we lost one market we got the other, and that is the advantage of having two markets. You cannot have it both ways. When the British market is bad, it is an advantage to have the United States market. But who is losing the British market now? I might just as well castigate this government on that score. When the United States market prices become attractive naturally our cattle gravitate to the United States in spite of their high American tariff but this year we have shipped to the United Kingdom only between 5.000 and 6.000 head-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-and if the quota next year is based on our shipments this year we shall be limited to shipping 5,000 or 6.000 head to the British market. So there is no use in the minister indulging in these bedtime stories about our losing markets because if we lost one we gained the other, and we did not lose the American market as the result of any action on our part but because the American government conceived that the action they took was the proper thing to do for the protection of their own farmers. But the Liberal government did do something to gain the British market by removing the embargo in 1923.

On each occasion that I have made reference to this matter I have been careful to state this, and I did so specifically in the house the other night, that we were not accusing hon. gentlemen opposite of losing the market but simply that the market was lost when hon. gentlemen opposite were in power, and that we objected to them blaming us for losing the market.
What could we have done to retain it?
I did not say you could have done anything.

Then what is the
use of chewing the fat about it?

The minister says that
it was under Liberal rule that we lost our market for cattle. Anyone who knows anything about raising cattle in western Canada knows that there is only one market for cattle, and that is the United States, and that market was lost in 1911 when the Conservative party defeated reciprocity. There is no doubt about that. Anyone who knows political history knows that that is when we lost our market. More than that, the American government kept the terms of the reciprocity pact open for our acceptance up to 1919, when we had a Conservative-Union government in power, and it would not accept it. After that government went out of power and a Liberal government came in here, we had a Conservative government in office across the line. Now we have a Democratic government in office across the line which is willing to give us a measure of reciprocity, and our government here says that we are going to have reciprocity. What I want to know is why we are not having it. Why is this government not doing something about it? They have told us for the last two or three years that they are negotiating with the United States for reciprocity, but it is just another promise like those they made five years ago. We all remember the wonderful things that they were going to do then. The farmer was going ,to get wonderful prices for his eggs and butter and wheat, and there was going to be heaven on earth, but it has turned out just the opposite. The farmers have learned what this government and its promises mean. I believe it is necessary to correct that situation. I believe it is necessary to have an organization in this country to study the matter and to watch it very carefully. We are out of the British market to some exent, if not altogether, because of the exports of the United States, and nobody yet knows whether that is a permanent export or not or whether something will happen, something that others may do or that may depend- on natural and other conditions in other countries, to bring about the conditions of 1923 or 1929.
The favorite policy of most people is to expand the markets in order to absorb the surplus. What if we -cannot do that? We have heard a good deal about grain mining, and whether or not it is a just phrase to use in connection with grain farming, we all know that any country which has continuously produced grains has usually had to quit that system and go in for mixed farming, where there is live stock and particularly cattle. I do not think there is any country in the world that has done more in the same number of years to improve its live stock than some of the ranchers in Canada have done, and the plight in which they have found themselves in the last five years has been desperate. Because of its importance to the national economy, because of its importance to the continued welfare of agriculture, I believe that a deliberate effort should be made to deal with any future problem of surplus in at least as effective a way as was done in regard to the wheat problem of this country.

In connection with bacon grading for export, a recommendation has been made by the price spreads commission that only graded and select hogs should be allowed to go into the product exported. About a year ago it was decided that definite grades should be set up in connection with bacon that was being exported from this country in order that we might overcome some of the criticism that had been made, to the effect that much of our bacon was not a credit to the Canadian people and had a detrimental effect on other prices obtained for the rest of the bacon in the old country. This has proved to be a difficult matter, especially considering the varied feeds used and the varied conditions that exist from one end of Canada to the other; it has been considered difficult to set definite standards in connection with bacon for export in view of these circumstances. It was felt at one time that only the top grade should be sent over, that a selection should be made of the best bacon processed and that this only should be ex-

ported. But those in the best position to advise, not only those personally interested but others as well, claimed that if we set a top standard only and set it too high there would not be sufficient of our bacon going into the United Kingdom to supply the demand that might be created for it. The endeavour was to hit a happy medium so that a sufficient quantity would go forward to meet the demand and at the same time as far as .possible not be detrimental to the reputation of Canadian packers.
There were three grades established first. They have been carefully checked on this side and also on the other side in the reception they have received from consumers in the old land.. After some time the three grades were cut to two, and now only two grades are going forward. On the basis of putting in selects and bacon that would be graded, say on the hoof, there would be no assurance that they would give the best finish, because the quality depends on the finish, and that cannot be told by those who would grade the hogs on the hoof. The hon. member will remember a letter I showed him this morning in this connection ; it was a confidential letter and cannot be read into the record of the house. He was not sent to a position in England, because he is still on the staff of the Department of Agriculture in Canada, but to make confidential reports. The value of his work has been much greater than we even expected when he went over, because by his manner and tact he has had a very fine reception and has received every assistance from every person on the other side as well as those in the trade. He writes directly to the packers who are sending over bacon that is not what it should be. He is candid in his criticism and in pointing out the criticisms that are made over there. Not satisfied with that a further barrage of promises by the Prime Minister was hurled across Canada over the ether waves shortly after the new year, another plethora of promises which have flattened out like the proverbial pancake or a busted tire. maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932

speechtext:
The house resumed from Friday, April 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. 13, to amend The Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act,	1932

Mr. Coote-Mr. Morand in the chair.
On section 1-Surrender of policy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Now observe that of that total over $61,000,000 has been loaned by companies beyond the legislative jurisdiction of this parliament. While we have licensed them under circumstances which I shall not now discuss, it will be readily understood that when they are advised

as they promptly will be, as it is their business, and they have agents who watch that sort of thing-when they are advised that we have passed legislation by which we have modified to any extent at all the terms of the contract made between the policyholder and the company, the credit of Canada suffers a great injury.
I say that with very great deliberation because I know whereoif I speak. Only a few years ago we endeavoured by a special form of taxation to do what had been done in other countries, and we were advised at once, almost by cable shall I say, that certain conditions that attached to certain contracts clearly must not be covered by such legislation.
Let me go further. The premium loans, that is, loans standing to the credit of policies in this country, to carry the policies forward when the unfortunate policyholders can no longer pay the premiums, so far as the Canadian companies are concerned amount to $33,564,616; in the case of British companies, to the small sum of $466,377, and in the case of foreign companies to $3,439,173. making a total for automatic premium loans of $37,470,166. So, sir, the total sum of these two amounts, or should I say the total amount of these two sums, is $244,746,378.
When I first saw those figures, Mr. Chairman, I confess that I was astonished. Here we have nearly a quarter of a billion dollars advanced on the security of the reserves, on policies or under contracts between the policyholders and the companies themselves. What do you think the statutory reserves, set up under the provisions of the Insurance Act, amounted to? As of December 31 they amounted to the very large sum of $1,224,650,970. That was the sum total of the reserves, so you will observe that of those reserves there had been drawn out in cash or set aside to meet premiums when the policies, in the familiar language of the home, had lapsed, about twenty per cent of the whole. In other words, of the reserves set up for the purpose of taking care of the Obligations of the companies, under policies of insurance, to widows, orphans and beneficiaries in this country, twenty per cent had been advanced to the policyholders or set aside to automatically carry forward the policies.
That is within Canada. Now let us proceed outside of Canada. -Canadian companies outside of Canada had loaned their policyholders $90,248,660 as of the end1 of December last-, and .automatically there had been provided $15,238,728, making a total of $105,487,388 against total reserves on the same policies of $693,281,773. So the companies doing business in Canada, Canadian companies doing business within and without our own country, the total loans on policies amounted to $235,663250 and automatic loans to $48,803,344, or a grand total of $284,466,594 against a reserve of $1,505,856,108. I ask my hon. friend from Macleod and the members of this committee: At this moment, when the insurance companies are willing to enter into an agreement with the minister, and lodge it in has office, that they will reduce their rate on all outstanding loans to six per cent and make the same rate on all future loans as of January 1-and it will be the subject matter of further discussion as time proceeds-with further loans amounting to $105,000,000 outside of this country, where reserves have to be set up, do you think we should have it said that this dominion took this action to-night with respect to these contracts, without any consultation with the policyholders and against the legal position taken by the insurance companies who are willing, however, to notify their policyholders that they will make the agreement to which I have referred?
I have only one further observation to make upon another phase of the question. I did point out that it is inimical to the interests of those who are to be protected by insurance that loans should be made against the policies. I do not suppose it is necessary to argue in this committee, where there are a great many gentlemen who have outstanding policies payable to their wives and children, how undesirable it is that the protection thus afforded should be reduced by loans, for unfortunately there is a tendency on the part of those who secure loans not to repay them -but to let the interest accumulate until such time as the reserves are wiped out. Let me give an illustration of how marked has been the borrowing of money in days of great prosperity, not for the purpose of paying premiums but for the purpose of engaging in hazardous undertakings and speculative enterprises. In the year ending December 31, 1924, we had loans in Canada against policies
Insurance Companies Act

amounting to $90,298,571, and the total policy-reserves were $585,596,956, the ratio of loans to reserves being 15-4 per cent. During the ensuing five years of very great speculative activity the loans increased to $159,353,195, as of December 31, 1929, and the reserves to $975,113,290, increasing the ratio of loans to reserves to 16-3 per cent. During the years of great depression from 1929 to 1934 loans on policies increased to $244,746,378 and total reserves to $1,224,650,970, and the ratio of loans to reserves to approximately 20 per cent. This indicates, of course, that in times of depression this reserve is available for any purposes for which it may be required, and much money has been drawn for those purposes during that time.
Now may I say to this committee that we have passed through five pretty bad years, and during some of that time we have had considerably increased responsibilities because securities decreased greatly in value and the reserves of the companies could not be readily realized upon without taking great losses. The demand for loans was so great that the premium income could not be invested but had to be utilized for the payment of loans upon policies or for cash surrender value of policies, and the result was that there was a rather acute condition, not only in this country but in every country. Particularly was that so in the United States where, as I dare say you have observed from the newspapers, some of the great companies met with very great difficulties indeed. Under those circumstances I suggest to the hon. gentleman that we should avoid again thrusting the insurance question into litigation. We have done the best we could, believing that the action was. legal, but having regard to the terms of the judgment of the privy council I am not expressing the certain opinion that there might not be grave difficulties in supporting some of the clauses of our statute. I would avoid it if we could, because the companies in which you and I have our money invested are most anxious that they should have dominion registration, that dominion licences should be forthcoming, that dominion investigations should take place and that the restrictions upon investments for insurance companies, which we have in the insurance acts, should be observed. If that is to be continued we must support and protect this legislation. We believe it is legal, but we desire to avoid litigation, and I may say that the legislation as it stands has met with the approval of the insurance companies themselves who, for the reasons I have indicated, are anxious that they should have dominion licences. Then again, I ask, is it desirable 
with respect to these companies transacting business both abroad and at home, where provision has been made to meet the situation, that those companies by legislative act should be compelled to do something which at this moment they are not prepared to do to the extent the hon. gentleman wishes? In other words having regard to the contracted sphere of sound investments and to the low price of government securities they have done what they could by the rates I have indicated to create a habit of not borrowing on insurance policies so that those policies may be maintained for the purposes for which they were originally taken out, namely for the protection of the beneficiaries named.
One more point, and I shall have concluded. It is this, that if we are to pass this legislation, let us do it by amending the Interest Act and not the Insurance Act. If it is the view of the house or committee that this is the time at which to reduce the rates, then I suggest that it be done in the way	I have indicated.
I have nothing to say against rates being reduced, so far as that is concerned. I desire to say only this, that it is not desirable to do so without the consent at least of one of the parties to an insurance contract; for what assurance have you or I that we are representing John Smith regarding the terms of his contract instead of John Smith himself? John Smith has agreed that the insurance company which makes the advance to him shall be able to take from him a rate of interest which shall not be greater than a certain amount. The agreement provides exactly what it is to be. How am I to say, "I can do better for John Smith and know more about his business than he does himself?" I know what some hon. gentlemen will say to that argument, but we must remember that this is a matter of an exact contract for each specific case, each loan which I have mentioned. Do hon. members think this parliament, or does the hon, member for Macleod believe that this parliament, should take that contract, tear it to pieces, and say, "This is the contract by which you are governed, and not that one?" If we desire to do it, let us make it a general act for the future.
Every man who has a policy of insurance has two interests, one of which is its safety. If it is a profit bearing policy it is a better policy when he dies than it was when he took it out. This very provision for interest enures to the benefit of every policyholder throughout the country. That is an amazing feature of it because it strengthens the re-

Insurance Companies Act
serve on his policy. Let me ask this further question: Is it desirable to take the action suggested at this particular time? Is it not desirable that we should adopt the reasonable method and, if we are to take action at all, place it in the statute relating to interest so that it shall apply to all? Countries abroad, whether they be Mexico, China or South America, would not be able to say that with respect to loans what we had done was not proper, but rather that under the interest law of Canada owing to the cheapness of money and the lowering of interest rates the rate had been reduced for general application to all companies, whether they were provincial or federal, foreign or British. There is standing in committee a bill which would enable such amendment to be made, if it be thought desirable. I do suggest however that the desirable course at this time is for us to accept the undertaking of the insurance companies to make the agreement with the superintendent of insurance, so that every policyholder may be advised that the company is now prepared to reduce the interest rate on his past agreements-as they are prepared to do unless he desires to do otherwise-and on future loans. There is one phase of the matter that I mention with great hesitancy, and that is that the suggested legislation may place a very serious strain upon the companies themselves in providing cash to meet the requirements of the policyholders, either for cash surrender values on the one hand or loans on the other.
There are amplifications of the reasons which I could give, but I have endeavoured to outline to the hon. member and hon. members of the committee what is in my mind, not because I am against the reduction of interest rates but because I am deeply solicitous about the future of Canada, its position among the countries of the world in connection with the maintenance of what may be good or bad at the time it is made, and the maintenance of legislation under which companies have issued contracts to various people in different parts of the world.
In suggesting the action I have indicated I do so with the full realization that it may readily be misunderstood. I feel however I would be recreant to my duty if I did not rise in my place to-night and indicate to the committee how serious I believe the result would be if we were to say to each individual policyholder in the world that we know better than he does how he should conduct his business with respect to his home and family, and the protection he affords to those he desires to protect, and in connection with the 92582-218
making of loans, whether automatic or otherwise on the reserves which have accumulated on his policy. If the hon. member will accept that view, very well, but if he does not accept it I think he must in all fairness resort to the provisions of the Interest Act, and not the Insurance Act, to protect us against attacks which might properly be levelled against us. If he accepts my suggestion, we may hope that even further concessions may be obtained by action of policyholders themselves, and we know that at least we shall have secured a fixed rate, a rate not exceeding six per cent, covering all charges of every kind in connection with advances which may be made against your accumulation and mine on money which we have entrusted to various companies to invest, against the contingency provided, namely the payment to the beneficiary of a sum named either as an endowment or a claim maturing at death.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Speaking on behalf of John Smith may I say that the member for Temis-oouata (Mr. Pouliot) has had experiences that quite probably the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) never had. I have often borrowed money from insurance companies, and I have found that the rate has been very high. When a man applies for a loan from an insurance company he does not discuss the rate of interest. He gets the money from the insurance company because he needs it badly, and the insurance company proceed to take advantage of that fact and charge the rate they wish. May I tell the Prime Minister, for his information, that when John Smith or John Doe goes to an insurance company to get money he has to comply with the conditions imposed by that company. Those conditions are not always pleasant, but when one needs money he must accept them as they are. That is a point which I suggest should not be overlooked.
Perhaps other hon. members have been in the same unfortunate circumstances and have had to borrow on their insurance policies. Undoubtedly they have found the rate very high. How is it that when rates of interest *have been reduced everywhere, insurance companies continue to impose their own high rates? How it it that when the government obtains the privilege of borrowing money at a low rate, individuals cannot do so? This is another point which cannot be understood by the common people. We know that in the first instance the rate of interest was reduced to the federal government; then it was reduced to the provincial government, and now the municipalities have obtained a lower rate of interest. But when it comes to an indiitEVISED EDITION
Insurance Companies Act

vidual, he must pay a high rate; the sky is the limit. Why do we have this discrimination? I find the condition I have described very hard to understand. I cannot understand the people who seek cheap money on the markets of the world and then tell the private individual that to save his country he must pay a high rate of interest. It is absurd, in my humble view, and I cannot understand it coming from a 'business man of the calibre of the Prime Minister. If the rate of interest is to be low for the federal government, if it is to be low for the provinces and the municipalities, it should be equally low for the private individual, and the reason why so miany individuals cannot pay their debts is because of the interest payments on their liabilities. It is a vast problem. I admit that the precise rate of interest fixed by the hon. member for MacLeod (Mr. Cootie) may be a matter for debate, but on the other hand something should be done t,o lower the rate of interest for the private individual. That is a matter of the utmost importance and it should be settled by this house because the usury act is an act of the parliament of Canada.
One reason why I do not object too strongly to this bill is that it is a public bill which affects all the insurance companies. I am strongly opposed to all private legislation to the granting of special privileges to this company and to that one. The business of parliament is to look after the general welfare of Canadian citizens as a whole, and we should not allow ourselves to be imposed upon by the private legislation which comes before us and which brings here swarms of lobbyists who are a pest to this house. Men who cannot earn anything before the courts come here and go from room to room canvassing in the interests of private legislation. It is shameful, because that legislation is to grant special privileges to the few. That is the sort of legislation I object to, but in a general way I do not object to public legislation by private members. That is our privilege. The members are here to enact legislation that affects every Canadian citizen. Therefore I think in principle the legislation which has been proposed by the hon. member for Macleod should receive the general approval of this house with the understanding that its particulars are a fair subject for debate.
The insurance companies always are complaining that their privileges are being curtailed. No one can expect that these companies, which have such enormous assets-and it is a good thing that they have-will be glad and that they will congratulate the House of Commons when by act of parlia-

ment their revenues are curtailed and the rate of interest is reduced on the loans which they make to their policyholders. On the other hand the public interest must be kept in view all the time, and it is on behalf of the man in the street who has to borrow on his insurance policy that I make these remarks to this committee.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I should like to ask
one question of the Prime Minister. He referred to one Canadian company doing business outside Canada, and said that it had loaned money in outside countries and that a high rate of interest was received upon its loans in certain countries. Can he tell us what rate of interest this company receives from the loans it makes in England, for instance?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext: Presumably the rate on policy loans of any company doing business in England would fee the going rate in England. The rate as fixed in 1910 was based upon the rate fixed in the Bank Act on the assumption that money should be borrowed on an insurance policy at a slightly higher rate than from the bank. The policy of 1910, and it is still the policy, was to discourage these loans being made. In England the rate of interest is much less than it is here, although I have not the figures; so is the interest rate on reserves, and so are the promises with respect to profits. One of the reasons our companies do a large business abroad is that they are supposed to have a good field for investment in Canada where the yield would be larger than in older countries where the rate of interest from securities is smaller; but with a reduction of the rate of interest on securities the profits on insurance policies have been reduced. The rate of interest varies in other countries and it varies here from time to time. When we fixed the rate in 1910 we did it with the purpose of not facilitating policy loans, the purpose being, as I have said, to maintain a slightly higher rate on policy loans than money might be obtained for from a bank or other lending institution, in order to discourage the practice. I remember a friend of mine saying to me in this house that he wished that ten years ago there had been a law prohibiting loans on policies, for he had made a loan and had not been able to repay it-he wished he had never been able to get it.

maintopic: CANADIAN AND BRITISH INSURANCE COMPANIES ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must say that the Prime Minister's statement to-night came as a complete surprise to me. I had no intimation, no knowledge of it at all; in fact I did not expect the insurance com-

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
panies would make such a proposal to the government, and naturally I feel that I would like to have the opportunity of seeing in Hansard the statement made by the Prime Minister and possibly of seeing the suggestion which the insurance companies have made to the government.
As to the propriety of the house dealing with the .matter I may say that the insurance companies were very ably represented before the banking committee by Mr. Rowell, and speaking from memory I understood him to say that so far as this particular section of my bill is concerned, fixing the rate of interest on future contracts, we are certainly within our rights. That is, he did not raise any question of constitutionality at all in regard to that section. As the section was originally drawn I believe he did suggest that it might be regarded as perhaps outside the powers of parliament, but the redrafted bill as it was passed by the committee makes it clear that the rate of interest this bill seeks to impose would apply only to loans made after the first day of January, 1936. That will be clear, I think, upon a reading of the bill. It says:
No company shall charge, stipulate for, or recover as interest in respect of any loan made to any person on a policy of insurance issued or effected upon the life of any person-
I draw particular attention to the words that follow:
-resident in Canada at the time the policy was issued or effected, any amount in excess of five per centum per annum, compounded annually, on the balance of the loan from time to time unpaid by the borrower.
I just mention that to make it clear that this was not to apply to any policies or any loans made outside of Canada, and in that particular the committee was very careful [DOT] to see that the bill as passed by them did not infringe upon that right. I hope that before the bill is up again I may have the opportunity of studying the statement which the Prime Minister has placed upon Hansard.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock the minister was dealing with the question of the fixing 92582-218J
of prices for potatoes under the potato marketing board, and I was asking him if he had had any opinion from the Department of Justice intimating that there was power for an agency of the kind which appears to have been appointed here to fix prices or to issue an order to the dealers that a certain price must be obtained. I understood the minister to say that that point had not come up I am wondering whether during the recess the minister has looked into the matter and found an answer, and whether he can give us now the benefit of any information he has gathered.

My information is that the Justice department has not been asked for its opinion as to whether or not the central marketing agency had the power to fix a price. As regards the other question with respect to the personnel of the board, on the local potato board, which includes two from Quebec, six are growers: J'. J. Trainor, Prince Edward Island; R. K. Lougheed, Nova Scotia; F. I. Boates, Nova Scotia; G. C. Cunningham, New Brunswick; J. T. Cassin, Ontario; C. E. Broughton, Ontario. Two are shippers; M. G. McNealy, Prince Edward Island; H. L. Mulharin, New Brunswick. Three are connected with growers' organizations: W. J. Tawse, Quebec; J. H. Lavoie, Quebec; L. F. Burrows, chairman.

The minister has said that the Department of Justice had not been asked whether or not the central marketing agency had authority to fix a price. By the central marketing agency, did he mean the agency appointed by the local board?
Yes.
The minister agrees, I presume, that the local board itself has no power to fix prices.
Yes.

Has he not taken an opinion or given consideration to the question whether or not the local board, not having the power to fix prices, may indirectly fix prices by appointing a marketing agency which does so? Does he think that the agency can do what the board itself cannot do?
There is no doubt that the agency can do certain things which the board cannot do.
For instance?

For instance, the agency can market and the local board can-

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
not. With reference to the hon. member's question regarding the fixing of prices, I think he will agree that the term "fixing of prices" is capable of different interpretations. The agency is appointed by the local marketing board in this particular instance for the purpose of marketing potatoes through that agency. The agency, in the ordinary course of selling, Would decide as to what was considered the best method, under conditions such as prevailed, of getting the largest returns to the producer, and in so doing he would doubtless offer at a certain price the product he had to sell. If that price were found to be such that the product would not move freely, or that its movement would be handicapped in merchandising, the agency would naturally change the price. As I say, "fixing of prices" is open to different interpretations. Personally I see nothing wrong with the action which was taken, especially under these conditions.

I do not want to prolong the debate if it is going to get into a legal discussion, but the minister is speaking of a commercial transaction. The transaction which takes .place here is not in. any sense, as I understand it, a marketing transaction by the agency. Take Mr. Cunningham, for instance: all that he does is to issue an order to certain dealers throughout the province declaring, "You shall sell your goods for so much." If that price is fixed too high the result very often is that the goods do not go into consumption as quickly as would be the case otherwise, and when that happens very often you have left a surplus which does not go into consumption at all but which is left on the hands of the seller to spoil. There is just one other matter I wish to refer to. We were discussing it last night when the house adjourned. The discussion brought up a ruling given by the Saskatchewan court of appeal and the minister interjected into my remarks that "that case did not refer to the provisions of the marketing act; it had nothing to do with the marketing act," and I replied "I know that." But I spoke too soon. I did not mean to say that it had nothing to do with the marketing act, but that it had nothing to do with the marketing act directly. The minister must surely admit that the case was a very clear one, and that it did strike at the very root of the marketing act. The actual case was brought up under the Live Stock Act, but the point was that this appeal court decided that this system of trying to pass enabling legislation was ultra vires. I have the case in front of me here. It is reported in the Western Weekly Reports of May 4, at page 34. It is the case of Rex versus Zaslavsky. It appears that he is a dealer who bought some cases of eggs and did not comply with the regulations made under the Live Stock Act of this parliament. The case was appealed and a stated case was presented to the court, asking three specific questions: (1) Whether the Live Stock Act of Canada and the regulations thereunder were valid and binding on the accused; (2) if not, were they valid and binding on the accused by reason of the Live Stock Products Act passed by the Saskatchewan government; (3) was the governor in council empowered under the Live Stock Act of Canada to enact prohibition in regard to purchasing of eggs as contained in clause 9 (4) of the regulations. I have put the questions briefly in my own language. The answer in the case of the first two questions was no, that both the act and the regulations sought to be enacted by the Dominion of Canada were ultra vires, and so they were under the provincial act.
The minister I think said last night that I wmuld find if I looked at the case that the objection taken was to the manner in which the enabling legislation was passed, but I think
the language used was that customary in all these cases. The judgment said:
It was provided that any provision of the dominion act ... within the legislative authority of the province, and outside that of the Dominion of Canada, shall have the force of law in Saskatchewan, and. unless otherwise enacted by the legislature of Saskatchewan shall be and remain in full force and effect therein to all intents and purposes whatsoever, until the same is repealed by the dominion parliament.
Then in the article there is this remark:
This phraseology is used in nearly all provincial enabling statutes.
I believe that that is practically the language generally used. Well then, if it has been decided, although not of course finally because no doubt the case will go to the privy council, bv an appeal court in the province of Saskatchewan that this system of passing enabling legislation is all wrong and ultra vires, I ask the minister and his officials whether that does not strike at the very root of the marketing act when it. is admitted that we here have not sole jurisdiction nor has the province, and we try to get around it by passing enabling legislation. I think the province of British Columbia passed legislation along somewhat similar lines. If the only legal decision up to date of any value going beyond magistrate's court is the one I have just cited, and that cannot be denied, what is the advice of the minister as to the legal status of the marketing act?

In the first place, Mr. Chairman, I have no advice to give in that connection. What I had reference to last night was that this was dealing specifically with the marketing act. The judgment given found the court divided.
With the chief justice siding with the majority.

Yes. The case has been brought to the attention of the Department of Justice. I think everyone who has given any special attention to the question of a lot of this legislation, and the benefit of it while it has been in operation, realizes that it is a matter of the very first concern that all these acts do operate to a certain extent on the basis of enabling legislation. Under the marketing act there are certain things that can be done without enabling legislation of the province, but they may not be as complete and effective as if enabling legislation were passed. The matter is, as I stated before, under advisement by the Department of Justice. What, their opinion is I do not know. I do not think they have come to a decision yet.

Last night, speaking on this bill, the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) went out of his way to deliver a campaign speech and he was allowed a great deal of latitude. I have no fault to find with that, but I expect to have the same privilege extended to me in discussing some of the subjects he dealt with. Some of the things the hon. gentleman said I heartily agree with. For example, he referred to the critical position of agriculture at the present time, and I absolutely agree with him. The agriculturist is indeed in a critical condition throughout the dominion wherever I have been, not only in the west but in eastern Canada as well. I agree with him also when he says that unless agriculture is made prosperous no industry can prosper. We gre not yet out of the depression, and until agriculture is. put on a sound and prosperous basis once more the country at large will not be prosperous. When the hon. gentleman says that Canadian agriculture must be made prosperous once more if Canadian industry generally is to return to prosperity, I heartily agree with him; but immediately after that, or at any rate during his speech, he began to advise the farmers of the west how to farm. I take

issue with him there. Let me tell him first of all that the man who comes from the east, even though- he may be a good farmer, will find it necessary to live in the west for one or two years at least before he knows how to farm-yes, before he knows how to farm.
Oh, oh.

It is all very well for you to laugh, but I have seen better farmers than you come out west and they have discovered after two or three years that at first they had not known how to farm. I have farms in three or four different parts of western Canada and in no two sections do I farm land in the same way. In some places the land has to be farmed with a view to the consequences of drought; in other places the farmer has to take preventive measures against frost; in other sections again the land has to be farmed so as to keep down, weeds, and so on. And when you come from eastern Canada knowing nothing about the conditions in the west and presume to tell us how to farm, well you have another guess coming. There are no better farmers anywhere in this world to-day than the western farmer, nor more intelligent. He knows how to farm, and he has taken the best methods of farming his land. All he wants, and he is demanding it, is that eastern Canadian industry shall get off his back and give him a chance to live. Get off his back and gjive him a chance to get along, and he will! do so without subsidies or any help in the form of marketing schemes. He does not need these things. The hon. gentleman spoke about bonuses given to farmers, how they bonusedl them to the tune of 820,000,000 or $25,000,000 in connection with freight rates, or something of that sort. Let me remind him that we paid in Saskatchewan in the year 1931 the sum of $29,000,000 in order to keep up Canadian industry. That is to say, we paid $29,000,000 more than we should have paid for the goods we purchased in the west, all on account of tariffs and other restrictions put on against us which prevented us from importing the things we needed. Not that we paid that duty; I do not mean that. I mean that we paid that much more to industry in Canada for our goods because of the duties and the restrictions which were imposed upon us. We were unable to buy in the cheapest markets, world markets, but had to buy under the conditions laid down by these tariffs and restrictions. Again I say, get off our backs and let us have a chance;
let us buy these things in the open market. Some of you say that you have low tariffs, that the Liberals had much higher tariffs than the Conservatives.
Sure.

Sure they did; and I suppose you will tell them at the same time that you reduced -the tariff on liquor from S10 to $5 a gallon. And to make up the difference, what did you do? You put two-cents a pound on sugar, and then you reduced it to one cent-you were ashamed of yourselves. Now we need money in this country, and if people w^ant to drink liquor they have a Tight to pay a duty to the government. But when you put it on a necessity such as sugar and take it off liquor, a great deal of explanation to the people throughout the country is needed.
You did the same thing with cigarettes, and then you thought: Well, the fellow in the backwoods is so poor he has begun to roll his own, and so you went to work and put a tax on the paper, but you did not put it on the paper that the Imperial Tobacco Company is using; you let them go free. The poor fellow in the back concessions who buys his paper to roll his cigarettes has to pay the tax, while the poor Imperial Tobacco Company that is so hard up that it is paying $05,000, $35,000-, $40,000 a year to nincompoops and then on top of that paying bonuses of $25,000 or $30,000 a year, is let off easily because it is too bad to hurt such people! Somebody suggests: What about matches? The man who buys a two-bit lighter has to pay the extra ten cents; they wanted to drive him to using matches instead of lighters. That is the situation which exists in Canada to-day, yet the government says: How solicitous we are for the poor man on the back concessions! I do not know what the hon. member is talking about; I did not hear him so I cannot answer him. I say that the only open market we have, the market that has remained open for many years, is the English market, but day after day and week after week that market for our wheat has been lost. Why is it that Argentina has been able to increase her sales of wheat to England month by month during the past year and yet we are told that under our Ottawa agreements she must pay six cents a bushel duty before she can unload? Argentina has increased her exports to England while ours have gone down. Yet they tell us the Liberals lost it all. Let me tell you that the duty is of no account so far as France or Germany or certain European countries are concerned, because they are not allowed to import wheat except as they export some. Those
markets were all closed to us when we came into office.

Yes, I am telling you that, and are still. But we are selling to them practically as much as we ever sold because they have to have our wheat, and when they export a bushel they are allowed1 to import one free of duty. That is the only wheat they are allowed to grind in those countries. So it is restrictions as well as duties that block us. In most of those countries the restrictions mean that they have to use one hundred per cent of the wheat they grow themselves in order to make the flour they use, but if they bring in wheat in exchange for their own they are allowed to grind that.
As far as exporting cattle is concerned, England is too far away from us in western Canada. As to the export and sale of butter, certainly we are selling more from western Canada than we ever sold, and we are making more. Back in 1920 to 1930 the people were so prosperous that they did not bother to sell butter; they used it for their cooking. To-day they iare selling the butter and using dripping; they have to because they are so hard up. They have to do almost anything to make a nickel. This is a nickel government, that is what it is. Talk about a five cent piece; this government looks like a nickel 1 Well, the people of Canada figure it is time they called it quits and gave the people a chance to operate, and when they do it will be just too bad. They will never get over the operation; they will die on the table.

The hon. member introduced the tariff element into this discussion. Possibly that has not so much bearing on the Natural Products Marketing Act as we would like it to have, but it was mentioned by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell) and the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly). I asked the last speaker whether he thought that by lowering the tariff on all the items in the schedule we would restore our lost markets and find new markets for our wheat. When I asked that question the hon. member for Willow Bunch said I did not know what I was talking about.
Pardon me; what I said was that I did not know what you were talking about. I could not hear you.

I spoke quite loudly. Possibly the hon. member for Willow Bunch wanted to be conveniently deaf at the time I asked that question, because it is indeed pertinent to the subject he discussed. Up in my district farmers are asking that question every day, as to whether a lowering of the tariff would restore the European market for our Alberta wheat. According to my recollection, in 1920 a binder cost just as much as a binder costs at the present time, so out there we do not feel that the tariff has done as much for the farmers as the hon. member for Willow Bunch and others who hold the same views would like us to believe.
There are gentlemen in my district who are telling the farmers that if they elect a Liberal government not only will the old markets be restored but new markets will be found. I wonder where they are going to find new markets at the present time. Are they going to send that colossal genius Bob Deachman, who I understand is a candidate in one of the Huron ridings, and the hon. member for Wey-burn down to the Fiji islands to teach the natives there how to bake bread? Are they going to send the histrionic member for Vancouver Centre to inveigle them out of their present food habits? Or are thej^ going to employ the editorial pen of the lugubrious

gentleman from North Battleford to stop the Chinese raising rice and make shredded wheat and pancakes all the rage in that country? For the life of me I cannot understand where they are going to find these new markets. I believe there is an essential difference between Conservatism radicalism and Conservatism liberalism. I did not rise either to praise or to bury the government that introduced this marketing act. Personally I feel, like the hon. member for Melville', that this is a step in the right direction. Perhaps mistakes may have been made in certain particulars, but I certainly feel that it is a step in the right direction. It has been introduced from the point of view of what I have designated as conservative radicalism, and as between that and conservative liberalism I prefer the conservative radical application of the act as it is now presented to the House of Commons. After all, what is radicalism? It comes from the word "radix", which means the root. In other words radicalism means nothing more than going to the root of the problem, and I feel that this Natural Products Marketing Act goes to the root of the problem at the present time. I do not believe in the methods of those political dinosaurs and dodos who live in an age that is past, who still believe that by a policy of laissez-faire we can restore prosperity to this country. The farmers of my part of the country feel that we must approach this problem from a more radical point of view, whether that point of view be conservative radicalism or the point of view7 that we in this corner of the house have expressed. government must be brought into better coordination.

Mr. Chairman, I have
not taken up much time this session so I do not think I should be criticized for saying a few words now. On March 18 I requested certain information from the Minister of Agriculture, which he was kind enough to furnish. I made reference to the fact that last year in northern Ontario we had a bumper hay crop. Within the last three weeks I have visited nearly every section of that part of the country, and I must tell the committee that there are tens of thousands of tons of hay there unsold at the present time. The people in that part of the country, whether rightly or wrongly, blame the government for the present state of affairs so far as the hay market is concerned. I mentioned on a previous occasion that early last fall, after the farmers and settlers began to press their hay, we had in the Canadian market some American buyers. In those weeks our farmers were selling their hay on cars at an average price of S15 per ton. The minister was kind enough to tell us that the Americans took restrictions off the importation of hay to their own country, but that the federal government licensed the buyer. The reason indicated by the minister was that of maintaining a higher price. We know that last summer there was a drought in western Canada, and that to some extent the same con-

Supply-Agriculture-Marketing Act
dition existed in New Brunswick and Ontario. I do not believe the minister was explicit enough in the statement he made on March 18; his statement has not been clear enough to satisfy the people in my constituency. He stated that it would be impossible for us to ship our hay to the three western provinces affected by the drought. Due to the restriction imposed by the federal government, and the licensing of the American buyer, these agents in Canada immediately ceased to buy our hay. To-day it is a drug on the market; you cannot give it away.
I do not know whether or not the marketing act has affected the situation, but I must say that in the past twenty or twenty-five years we have paid very high prices for hay purchased in eastern Canada. In those days we did not obtain help from the federal government, nor was there any attempt made to help pay the price. At the present time the people in my constituency are paying more for Canadian wheat, Canadian flour and Canadian grain because of governmental activities. We do not begrudge the expenditure, because we want to see the western farmer prosper. But surely the federal government should not place a restriction against our agricultural production when practically the only natural market we have for our hay is in the United States. I know the minister wishes to be fair in his statement, but I must say to him sincerely that the statement he made was not satisfactory to my section of the country. If to-morrow we could sell the hay in northern Ontario at an average of $12.50 or $15 per ton, ninety per cent of our settlers would be taken off relief. They have to be maintained, however, because they cannot sell their hay crop.
I trust the minister will give a satisfactory answer to my question. I believe action has been taken which has had the effect of restricting hay export to the American market. I trust the minister will reply so that I shall be able to give a satisfactory answer to my constituents. I am not speaking politically, but am addressing the minister broadly and am taking the wider view. Undoubtedly the minister is well aware of my stand in the matter.
There is another point to which I should like to bring the minister's attention. When the people in my constituency buy fruit from the Niagara peninsula or from some other of the older sections of the province a flat express rate of 32 cents per basket is charged for transportation from those older sections to northern Ontario. Naturally we are satisfied with that charge, but when the people in northern Ontario wish to ship their natural
fMr. Bradette.]
fruits, such as blueberries, the gathering of which constitutes a local industry, and particularly at points such as Iroquois Falls and Porcupine, we find that we must pay a rate of more than 60 cents on baskets of the same size as those in which fruit is shipped from the older sections. The minister will readily appreciate that an injustice is done our shippers. The blueberry industry employs hundreds of people during the summer months when the fruit is ripening, and I believe the marketing board should take steps to adjust the rates on shipments from northern Ontario to the older sections of the province. The minister will readily realize what the rate means to the growers in the Porcupine district which at the present time has a population of nearly 50.000 people, and is increasing by leaps and bounds. I appreciate the opportunity now given me to correct what is no doubt a wrong impression concerning the restrictions placed upon the export of hay which, it is suggested, have interfered with the market in the hon. member's district. When I made my answer I had in mind the fact that due to the very high freight rates it would be impossible profitably to ship hay from his section of the country to western Canada. Last year there was a very definite scarcity of feed in certain districts of eastern and western Canada, and upon the representations of different organizations it was thought advisable to have some provisions whereby governments undertaking relief would not be left in such a position that there would not be sufficient fodder to feed live stock. The provision made to protect against this condition was a very generous one. Every possible effort was made to facilitate and expedite the issuing of a licence. Any man with a legitimate sale of hay could apply for a licence and in every case in eastern Canada I understand such licence was granted. No licences were refused, and I believe it was made clear that no licence would be refused to a man who had a legitimate sale of hay, unless conditions should arise where the scarcity of feed was such that there was not sufficient feed available to supply the live stock. Even then licences would not be refused but the province interested would be given permission to buy at the same price. I appreciate the oppor-

tunity the hon. member has given me, and I have confidence in his fairness. Undoubtedly he will take the first opportunity to correct any wrong impression in his constituency. I have made a note of his observations regarding express rates, but I must say that such matters would not come within the administration of the marketing act. The situation he has described seems almost incredible, and I appreciate his having brought it to the attention of the committee.

It is my understanding
of the act that a provincial board may prevent the products of one province from entering another.

That is not my
understanding. I believe there is no provision through which that restriction coulld1 be imposed.

There is no provision in
the act to that effect, but boards are given that jurisdiction. They may prevent the goods of one province from entering another.
I am afraid the hon. member is in error. I should be pleased to have him submit a specific instance.

Before the item is carried I have something further to say. This act is essentially parochial, and it is against the terms of the British North America Act. We have a Minister of Agriculture in Ottawa to facilitate trade between provinces and with other countries, and therefore the act in its present form is in my judgment against the spirit of the British North America Act. This is a very serious matter which I have brought to the attention of the committee. Soon we will have the opportunity to submit it to the people.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) moved the first reading of Bill No. 88, to amend the Admiralty Act, 1934.
He said:	May I explain, Mr. Speaker,
that in the Admiralty Act passed last session there is a provision that an appeal from the
local judge in admiralty shall be heard by two judges of the exchequer court. The president of the exchequer court has pointed out that it is very seldom there are two exchequer court judges in the city who could hear the appeal, and this amendment is merely to restore the old practice that such an appeal may be heard by one exchequer court judge.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
